## Verdict

**Answer:** Since 2022, deepfake research has expanded from detecting manipulated media toward broader, adversarially robust and multimodal detection. Fraud reporting increasingly describes deepfakes as one tool in impersonation and social engineering; the evidence here does not establish a comparable, measured increase in fraud caused by deepfakes.

**Decision:** Fund layered identity and transaction controls, with human verification for high-risk requests; treat deepfake detection as one signal, not a standalone fraud barrier.

**Confidence:** medium - research directions are documented, but this response has no live Prism query, systematic paper counts, or comparable news series.

**What would change it:** A reproducible, date-bounded search with deduplicated papers and a consistent news corpus that separates deepfake-enabled fraud from other fraud.

## What the data shows

This is a qualitative synthesis from published work I can identify from memory, not a counted literature review. I cannot provide a sourced annual paper count, citation momentum, or news trend. The references show a change in research questions: from detecting synthetic faces and manipulated video toward generalization to unfamiliar generators, provenance, and operational risks. Those works establish research activity and framing, not real-world detection accuracy or fraud incidence.

## Comparison

On a single qualitative scale—whether the cited works explicitly address the theme—the selected 2022 baseline has manipulation detection present and broader operational framing absent; the selected 2023–2024 works include both. This is a presence/absence comparison, not a ratio of papers, citations, or incidents. I cannot measure a field-wide delta from these examples.

## Evidence

## Verdict
- Answer: Since 2022 the field moved from detecting face-swap videos on curated benchmarks to a generalisation problem. Diffusion images, voice cloning and real-time video are the new targets. Fraud is now framed as an organisational and financial-control problem, not only a media-forensics one. Detectors lose much of their accuracy on real-world content, and humans are no better at spotting fakes.
- Decision: Treat detection as one layer only. Put resources into process controls (out-of-band callback, dual approval) and provenance, and test any detector on your own in-the-wild data before buying.
- Confidence: medium. The qualitative shifts are well documented in papers I know. This run used no Prism calls, so counts, citation numbers and news volumes are not measured.
- What would change it: Independent, field-based evidence that detectors hold their accuracy on new generators, or measured deepfake-specific loss data that contradicts the vendor and forecast figures used here.

## What the data shows
Nothing below was retrieved live. Every figure comes from a named published source or is labelled (est.).

- **Generalisation gap.** Deepfake-Eval-2024 tested open-source detectors on content collected in 2024. It reports AUC drops of about 50% for video, 48% for audio and 45% for images against older academic benchmarks [r6]. This is my recollection of the paper; verify before quoting.
- **Humans.** Observers rated AI-synthesised faces as indistinguishable from real ones, and more trustworthy [r4]. In a speech study, listeners detected deepfakes only about 73% of the time (est. from memory of [r5]).
- **Diffusion shift.** GAN-trained detectors failed on diffusion images [r1][r2]. Work on universal detectors then targeted cross-generator transfer [r3].
- **Audio.** Evaluation shifted to whether detectors generalise across datasets and conditions [r7]. The ASVspoof challenge series set the earlier baseline [r8].
- **Fraud loss.** The best-known single incident is a Hong Kong employee at Arup who transferred about US$25 million after a deepfake video call, reported in Feb 2024 [r11]. Deloitte forecast US generative-AI-enabled fraud losses rising from US$12.3 billion in 2023 to US$40 billion by 2027 [r9]. That is a forecast, not an observed count.
- **Vendor claims.** Sumsub reported roughly a 10x rise in detected deepfakes in 2023 versus 2022 [r10]. That is vendor data from its own customer base, so treat it as indicative only.
- **Overall fraud context.** FBI IC3 reported total reported cyber-crime losses of US$10.3B (2022), US$12.5B (2023) and US$16.6B (2024) [r12]. These are not deepfake-specific.

**New work since 2022** (citation counts are not measured here; see Method and limits):

| Work | Year | Orientation | Identifier |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nightingale & Farid, synthetic faces | 2022 | Critical of human ability | [r4] |
| Müller et al., audio generalisation | 2022 | Critical of detectors | [r7] |

**Momentum.** Publication volume since 2022 is not measured here. The direction is visible in the topics: generalisation, diffusion, audio and in-the-wild benchmarks replaced face-swap-only evaluation.

**Framing shift** (interpretation):
1. From "can we spot the artefact?" to "will it transfer to a generator we haven't seen?"
2. From media forensics to fraud, identity verification and business email compromise.
3. From detection alone to provenance and watermarking (C2PA, content credentials) and regulation, such as the transparency duties in the EU AI Act.

**Under-covered topics** (interpretation, not measured):
- Deepfake-specific loss statistics, because most figures are vendor or forecast numbers.
- Detector performance in live call and KYC pipelines.
- Human-plus-process defences, such as callbacks, compared against detectors.
- Low-resource languages in audio detection.
- Post-compression performance on messaging apps.

**News trend.** I cannot give a measured volume series. Landmark dated stories are the Arup case (Feb 2024) [r11], and the Jan 2024 New Hampshire robocall that cloned a presidential voice (est., reported widely; no reference given). Coverage appears to have moved from celebrity and political fakes toward corporate fraud, but this is not counted.

## Method and limits
- **Windows.** Research and news material covers 2022 to the end of 2025. The IC3 series ends with 2024, about 22 months before today (2026-10-23). The Deloitte forecast runs to 2027. I know of nothing from 2026 and did not search.
- **Lanes.** Research papers, industry and vendor reports, government statistics, and news incidents.
- **Coverage and censoring.** The sources are a hand-picked set recalled from memory, not a systematic sample. Figures from [r6] and [r5] are recalled and may be imprecise. Please verify them before use.
- **Match mode.** Not applicable, since no database query was run.
- **What the counts are and are not.** The IC3 totals cover all reported cyber-crime, not deepfakes. The Deloitte figure is a forecast. The Sumsub figure is vendor-observed and has an unclear denominator.
- **Cannot answer here.**
  - Citation counts per paper.
  - A measured publication trend.
  - A measured news-volume trend.
  - Deepfake-specific realised losses.
- **Interpretation.** The framing-shift and under-covered-topic sections are my reading, not counted.
